book: How Search Decides What You See
author: Aaron Tay

episodes.title: Where did the paper go?
episodes.subtitle: Locate the missing evidence before changing the query.

scenes.title: One symptom, several causes
scenes.claim: A missing result does not identify the failing stage
scenes.narration: You know a relevant paper exists. Your search does not show it. Should you add a synonym, change the model, or try again? First, locate where the evidence disappeared. Chapter thirteen treats the result screen as a symptom. Several different failures can produce exactly the same empty space.

scenes.title: Was it in the searchable collection?
scenes.claim: Coverage and indexing lag come before matching
scenes.narration: Our paper, P, is a hypothetical known relevant record. In this first case, it sits outside the searchable collection. The source is not covered, or indexing has not caught up. Query expansion cannot retrieve a record that is absent. Check coverage and indexing lag before inspecting its vocabulary.

scenes.title: Was it eligible under the limits?
scenes.claim: A covered record may still be excluded by a filter
scenes.narration: Now P is in the collection, but a date limit excludes it. A format facet or access filter could do the same. Investigate the actual metadata and applied limits. This is a different boundary from coverage. A paper can be indexed and still never enter the eligible set.

scenes.title: Did it enter the shortlist?
scenes.claim: Later reranking cannot recover an absent candidate
scenes.narration: Next, P is eligible, but the first retrieval stage does not supply it to the shortlist. Investigate the query, indexed evidence, retrieval method, and candidate cutoff. A reranker can rearrange the candidates it receives. It cannot promote a missing paper from a shortlist that never contained it.

scenes.title: Was it retrieved but hidden?
scenes.claim: Candidate membership and displayed results are different
scenes.narration: In the fourth case, P reaches the candidate pool, then falls below the display cutoff. It matched, but you did not see it. Inspect ranking, later selection, and presentation limits. An interface alone may hide these boundaries. Without documentation or a trace, record what remains unknown.

scenes.title: Was the evidence split apart?
scenes.claim: The indexed unit determines what evidence is available together
scenes.narration: There is another boundary inside a document. Suppose the system indexes separate passages. One contains the intervention, another the outcome. No single indexed unit may carry enough evidence to rank. Also check whether matching occurred in an indexed field or version that the displayed excerpt does not show.

scenes.title: Different words, related concepts
scenes.claim: Vocabulary mismatch is a query–record relationship
scenes.narration: Only after checking those boundaries, inspect the language. Heart attack recovery and rehabilitation after myocardial infarction use related concepts in different words. That is vocabulary mismatch. Both expressions may be familiar to the index and model. Different wording does not, by itself, establish an out of vocabulary problem.

scenes.title: Build a bridge, then test it
scenes.claim: BM25 does not itself turn different terms into synonyms
scenes.narration: Librarians build bridges with synonyms, controlled vocabulary, citation searching, and reformulation. Boolean OR makes a bridge explicit. B M twenty five ranks lexical evidence; it does not itself make these phrases synonyms. A suitably trained dense or hybrid route may help. Test the bridge against the known relevant record.

episodes.title: Missing words, or missing meaning?
episodes.subtitle: Separate index vocabulary, model tokens, representation, and transfer.

scenes.title: Out of whose vocabulary?
scenes.claim: Name the component before calling a string OOV
scenes.narration: A specialised identifier appears in a record, but searching it behaves strangely. Calling it too new is not a diagnosis. Ask, out of whose vocabulary? The lexical index, the model tokeniser, and the learned retrieval representation answer different questions. A string can survive one layer and fail at another.

scenes.title: Does the index preserve a matching term?
scenes.claim: Query and document analysis must be inspected together
scenes.narration: After lexical analysis, does the query term have a corresponding indexed term and posting list? If it does not, it supplies no direct lexical evidence. Inspect the field and both analysis paths. An identifier visible on screen may have been split or normalised before it entered the searchable index.

scenes.title: Encodable does not mean understood
scenes.claim: BERT example: rizzlord → ri / ##zz / ##lord
scenes.narration: The chapter's BERT example splits rizzlord into ri, double hash zz, and double hash lord. Those are known pieces, but not the decomposition a reader expects. Another tokeniser may split it differently. Encoding the pieces establishes representability. It does not establish a useful retrieval meaning for the complete expression.

scenes.title: Exact identity can determine relevance
scenes.claim: Illustration: DELULU-427 is different from DELULU-428
scenes.narration: Now exact identity matters. The chapter uses DELULU four twenty seven. Our illustration contrasts it with four twenty eight. Consistent lexical analysis, or a keyword field, can preserve the required identifier. A pooled dense representation may blur decisive differences. Keep an exact lexical route and test the actual representation.

scenes.title: Familiar words, unfamiliar retrieval situation
scenes.claim: OOD concerns training–deployment transfer
scenes.narration: Out of distribution asks a different question. Does what the retriever learned during training transfer to this deployment? Every word can be familiar while retrieval performs poorly. Neither a vocabulary mismatch nor an unknown token is required. Training and deployment may differ in queries, collections, or the relationship rewarded as relevance.

scenes.title: Three places to investigate shift
scenes.claim: Query style · corpus/domain · task/relevance
scenes.narration: Look for three sites of shift. Users may ask longer questions or use another register. The corpus may change discipline, language, or document type. The task may change too: finding one answer bearing passage differs from finding all studies meeting review criteria. Familiar terminology does not make those tasks equivalent.

scenes.title: One bad result cannot prove OOD
scenes.claim: Use comparative local evaluation to test suspected transfer
scenes.narration: One poor result cannot prove distribution shift, particularly when training data are undisclosed. Compare performance on a local query and relevance set. Look for systematic degradation tied to a setting or task. These bars are explicitly hypothetical, not measured model scores. Adding another synonym does not establish that transfer improved.

scenes.title: Choose an intervention for the suspected layer
scenes.claim: Inspect analysis; preserve identity; evaluate and adapt transfer
scenes.narration: Match the intervention to the evidence. Inspect fields and analysis for lexical loss. Preserve exact identity for identifiers. Test representation quality when tokens exist but meaning is weak. For suspected transfer, evaluate locally before adaptation, retraining, or replacement. Retain useful lexical or hybrid fallbacks. Several diagnoses may apply together.

episodes.title: All the words. The wrong relationship.
episodes.subtitle: Test direction, negation, composition, and the remedy itself.

scenes.title: A causes B is different from B causes A
scenes.claim: Nearly identical lexical evidence can express opposing relations
scenes.narration: Imagine searching for A causes B and receiving a passage saying B causes A. The same words appear, but their roles are reversed. This failure can happen without missing vocabulary or distribution shift. What determines relevance is the relationship between the pieces, and the retrieval method has failed to preserve it.

scenes.title: A small word can reverse the claim
scenes.claim: Does increase risk ≠ does not increase risk
scenes.narration: Compare the intervention does increase risk with the intervention does not increase risk. Their overlap is enormous. Their claims oppose each other. A bag of words score may treat them similarly. A single pooled vector can also blur a decisive local difference. Similarity alone does not establish the required logical relationship.

scenes.title: Co-occurrence is not the requested relationship
scenes.claim: Concepts appearing together need not participate in the same claim
scenes.narration: Two concepts can occur in one passage without participating in the relationship you need. Ordinary term conjunction checks presence; it does not fully bind subject, action, and object. Phrase and proximity controls preserve useful local order or adjacency. Adjacency alone still does not solve causality, negation scope, or relation binding.

scenes.title: Read the query and candidate together
scenes.claim: Cross-encoding offers more interaction, without a logic guarantee
scenes.narration: A cross encoder reads query and candidate jointly, giving it a stronger architectural opportunity to model relationships. Late interaction preserves more token evidence than one pooled vector, but still encodes the two sides separately. Neither architecture guarantees correct logic. Test controlled contrasts, and remember that reranking needs the right candidate first.

scenes.title: Four lenses, overlapping evidence
scenes.claim: Mismatch · named vocabulary · transfer · relationships
scenes.narration: The chapter's four lenses describe different kinds of evidence. Vocabulary mismatch compares query and record language. Out of vocabulary names a particular vocabulary. Out of distribution compares training and deployment. Composition asks whether relationships survive matching. They overlap. Do not treat them as four exclusive boxes or four remedies to try blindly.

scenes.title: Different methods preserve different evidence
scenes.claim: Boolean logic · lexical evidence · learned overall similarity
scenes.narration: Three reference approaches preserve different things. Strict Boolean preserves explicit logic over analysed terms. B M twenty five preserves lexical evidence, especially rare matching terms. Single vector dense retrieval preserves overall learned similarity. Each has blind spots. Learnt sparse retrieval and late interaction add other options. No first stage preserves everything equally well.

scenes.title: Change one suspected mechanism and compare
scenes.claim: A controlled contrast makes a diagnosis testable
scenes.narration: Begin with a known relevant record or a controlled contrast. Establish eligibility and candidate boundaries, then choose an intervention suggested by the evidence. Compare the resulting retrieval against the same written requirement. More visible results need not mean better relevance. Record the changed condition, what improved, and which plausible alternatives remain.

scenes.title: Diagnosis supplies hypotheses, not proof
scenes.claim: Locate evidence loss → test a remedy → document uncertainty
scenes.narration: A fluent summary cannot repair retrieval built on the wrong records. The librarian's practical tool is a disciplined evidence trail: what could be searched, where the record disappeared, which relationship failed, and what the intervention changed. Keep unknowns visible. Chapter fourteen turns those diagnostic hypotheses into measured comparisons of retrieval.
